title: Jeremiah 27:1–11
context: This word comes to Jeremiah from the LORD in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah. The LORD tells him to make bonds and bars and put them on his neck, and then to send word by the messengers who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah, for the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon. The message is plain: the LORD has made the earth and gives it to whom it seems right to him; he has now given these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, his servant, and the nations are to put their neck under the yoke of that king and serve him. Those who will not serve will be punished with sword, famine, and pestilence. They are not to listen to prophets, diviners, dreams, soothsayers, or sorcerers who say they shall not serve. The nation that brings its neck under the yoke may remain in its own land and till it. The yoke is the plain sign of serving the king of Babylon, not a symbol to be pressed beyond that. The WEB dates the word to the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, while the verses that follow address Zedekiah and the messengers who come to him. That tension is noted here and is not resolved; no claim is made about other wording, and the two reigns are not forced into one scheme. 2 Kings 24–25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 later tell of Judah’s subjection and fall; those accounts may be named without being blended with this charge.

verses.text: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,” The heading dates the word to the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign. The verses that follow, however, speak of messengers who come to Zedekiah. The tension is real in the text as it stands and should be noted, not smoothed away. No claim is made here about other wording, and the two names should not be forced into a single reconstructed date.

Arminian readers take the line as the book’s own heading for a word that Jeremiah received from the LORD, and they can live with the date question as an open tension rather than a problem to be solved in the notes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise receive the heading as the book’s date for this word, while leaving the relation to Zedekiah in the following verses unharmonized and without manuscript claims.

Shared ground: the word comes to Jeremiah from the LORD. The Jehoiakim–Zedekiah tension, if mentioned, stays hedged.

verses.text: the LORD says to me: “Make bonds and bars, and put them on your neck.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says to Jeremiah, “Make bonds and bars, and put them on your neck.” The sign is concrete and should be kept plain: bonds and bars on the neck, a yoke like that of a beast put to work, standing for serving another’s rule. Jeremiah is to wear what the nations will be told to accept.

Arminian readers take the command as a real act Jeremiah is to perform, a visible word for those who will see him, not a mere figure of speech with no wooden bars.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the bonds and bars as a real sign the LORD commands, placed on Jeremiah’s neck as the message itself in visible form.

Shared ground: the yoke is plain. The verse does not invite an elaborate symbolism beyond serving the rule the next verses will name.

verses.text: Then send them to the king of Edom, to the king of Moab, to the king of the children of Ammon, to the king of Tyre, and to the king of Sidon, by the hand of the messengers who come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then the bars are to be sent “to the king of Edom, to the king of Moab, to the king of the children of Ammon, to the king of Tyre, and to the king of Sidon, by the hand of the messengers who come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah.” The word is for Judah’s neighbors as well as for Judah, and it is sent through envoys already in Jerusalem to see Zedekiah. The verse assumes Zedekiah on the throne as the messengers’ host; that sits beside the Jehoiakim heading without being reconciled here.

Arminian readers hear a public word meant for several courts, carried by real messengers, a charge those kings can receive or refuse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same list as the LORD’s reach: Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon, addressed through messengers at Zedekiah’s court.

Shared ground: the audience is international, and Zedekiah is named as the king to whom the messengers have come. Identities of the envoys themselves are not given and should not be invented.

verses.text: Give them a command to their masters, saying, ‘The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says, “You shall tell your masters:
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah is to “Give them a command to their masters,” and to say, “The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says, “You shall tell your masters:” The envoys are to carry the LORD’s word back to their own kings. The God of Israel addresses those masters as the one who has the right to command them.

Arminian readers take the chain of speech as serious: a word from the LORD, through Jeremiah, through the messengers, to the kings, who remain responsible for what they do with it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, claiming the right to speak to foreign masters through this command.

Shared ground: the message is the LORD’s, not Jeremiah’s private advice to Judah alone. The verse is an opening, and the content follows.

verses.text: ‘I have made the earth, the men, and the animals that are on the surface of the earth by my great power and by my outstretched arm. I give it to whom it seems right to me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I have made the earth, the men, and the animals that are on the surface of the earth by my great power and by my outstretched arm. I give it to whom it seems right to me.” The claim under the yoke is creation and gift. The LORD made the earth and gives it to whom it seems right to him. The political charge rests on that prior right, not on Babylon’s virtue.

Arminian readers hear a real giving in history, the LORD’s right to assign lands, without treating every later act of a given king as morally approved.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same confession as the ground of what follows: the earth is the LORD’s by power and outstretched arm, and he gives it as it seems right to him.

Shared ground: God made the earth and gives it. The verse is not yet the naming of Babylon, but it prepares that gift.

verses.text: Now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant. I have also given the animals of the field to him to serve him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant. I have also given the animals of the field to him to serve him.” Nebuchadnezzar is called “my servant,” the one into whose hand the lands, and even the animals, have been given. The title names his role in this giving, not a claim that his every deed is righteous. How God relates to a foreign king used as his servant is already treated in the existing box at Judges 9:23.

Arminian readers take the giving as a real historical assignment, which the nations are now called to accept, while Nebuchadnezzar remains a responsible ruler, not a mere tool without a will.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same “I have given” as the LORD’s sovereign disposal of lands, and “my servant” as the title he assigns to the king of Babylon for this purpose. The existing box at Judges 9:23 may be consulted on God and such agents.

Shared ground: these lands have been given into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand. The yoke that follows is the plain form of that service.

verses.text: All the nations will serve him, his son, and his son’s son, until the time of his own land comes. Then many nations and great kings will make him their bondservant.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the nations will serve him, his son, and his son’s son, until the time of his own land comes. Then many nations and great kings will make him their bondservant.” Service to Babylon has a term: him, his son, and his son’s son, until the time of his own land comes, when the conqueror will himself be made a bondservant. The verse does not name those later kings, and identifications should not be invented or pressed.

Arminian readers hear both the present service and a real later limit. Babylon’s time will come; the charge to serve now is not a claim that Babylon’s rule is endless.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the limit as the LORD’s: service until the time of Babylon’s own land comes, after which many nations and great kings will bind the conqueror.

Shared ground: the nations will serve, and that service will not last forever. The “son” and “son’s son” may be left as the verse states them, without a reconstructed king list.

verses.text: “ ‘ “ ‘It will happen that I will punish the nation and the kingdom which will not serve the same Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and that will not put their neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon,’ says the LORD, ‘with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, until I have consumed them by his hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says he will punish “the nation and the kingdom which will not serve the same Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and that will not put their neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon,” “with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, until I have consumed them by his hand.” The yoke is again plain: the neck under Babylon’s rule. Refusal brings sword, famine, and pestilence, until they are consumed by that king’s hand.

Arminian readers take the warning as a real alternative set before the nations: serve and, as the next verse will say of those who submit, remain; refuse, and face this punishment. The choice is grave and is addressed to them as those who can still put their neck under the yoke.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same punishment as the LORD’s announced word against the nation that will not serve. Sword, famine, and pestilence are his means, until they are consumed by Babylon’s hand.

Shared ground: refusal of the yoke is met with those three blows. The yoke remains the plain sign of service.

verses.text: But as for you, don’t listen to your prophets, to your diviners, to your dreams, to your soothsayers, or to your sorcerers, who speak to you, saying, “You shall not serve the king of Babylon;”
verses.arminianNotes:
“But as for you, don’t listen to your prophets, to your diviners, to your dreams, to your soothsayers, or to your sorcerers, who speak to you, saying, “You shall not serve the king of Babylon;”” The foreign courts are warned off a whole class of voices that promise they will not have to serve. Prophets, diviners, dreams, soothsayers, and sorcerers are named together when they say that.

Arminian readers hear a real warning they can heed: those voices are not to be followed, however many of them agree that service is unnecessary.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same list as the LORD’s prohibition. The message “You shall not serve the king of Babylon” is not to be believed, whatever the source that speaks it.

Shared ground: the banned word is the denial of the yoke. The verse does not require a new contrast over true and false prophecy; the charge is already specific.

verses.text: for they prophesy a lie to you, to remove you far from your land, so that I would drive you out, and you would perish.
verses.arminianNotes:
“for they prophesy a lie to you, to remove you far from your land, so that I would drive you out, and you would perish.” The pleasant word is called a lie, and its end is removal, driving out, and perishing. The lie is not a harmless comfort; it would take them from their land.

Arminian readers take the lie as a real deception the nations can refuse. Listening would lead to exile and death; refusing the lie is still open to them in the charge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a lie whose outcome, if believed, is driving out and perishing, a result the LORD himself names as what would follow.

Shared ground: the prophecy that they shall not serve is a lie, and it is deadly. The verse explains why they must not listen.

verses.text: But the nation that brings their neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serves him, that nation I will let remain in their own land,’ says the LORD; ‘and they will till it and dwell in it.’ ” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
“But the nation that brings their neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serves him, that nation I will let remain in their own land,” and “they will till it and dwell in it.” Submission has a promised outcome: remaining, tilling, and dwelling in their own land. The yoke is still plain service, not a mystic image.

Arminian readers hear a real offer standing beside the warning: the nation that serves may remain at home, a path still set before these kings and before Judah.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same promise as the LORD’s: the nation that brings its neck under the yoke will be let to remain, till, and dwell in its land.

Shared ground: service now is the way to remain. The contrast in the unit is between the lie of escape and this hard, life-preserving submission.
